clinicalPearls: Congenital blue-grey macule or patch, most often over the lumbosacral area and buttocks, present at or shortly after birth
Very common in infants of Asian, African, Hispanic and other darker-skinned backgrounds
Represents dermal melanocytosis, the blue-grey colour arising from a Tyndall effect of deep dermal melanin
Usually fades spontaneously during early childhood and needs no treatment
Can be mistaken for a bruise, so accurate documentation is important to avoid inappropriate concern about non-accidental injury

Extensive, widespread or persistent lesions, or those combined with vascular birthmarks (phakomatosis pigmentovascularis), may occasionally signal an inborn error such as GM1 gangliosidosis or a mucopolysaccharidosis
Aberrant lesions over unusual sites such as the shoulders or face overlap with naevus of Ito and naevus of Ota
reference.pathophysiology: During embryogenesis melanocytes derived from the neural crest normally migrate to the epidermis, but in dermal melanocytosis some are arrested within the dermis. Light scattering by this deep melanin produces the blue-grey colour, and most lesions involute as the ectopic melanocytes gradually disappear during childhood. Extensive or persistent lesions can rarely accompany lysosomal storage diseases, in which impaired clearance is thought to allow the melanocytosis to persist.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis based on typical appearance and site
Careful documentation and photography for medico-legal and safeguarding purposes
Dermoscopy where the diagnosis is uncertain
Assessment for dysmorphism or organomegaly with metabolic screening if lesions are extensive or persistent
Mapping of the distribution and review for associated vascular malformation
redFlags: Lesions mistaken for bruising that raise safeguarding concerns, requiring careful documentation
Extensive or persistent melanocytosis with dysmorphic features or organomegaly suggesting a lysosomal storage disease
An associated vascular malformation indicating phakomatosis pigmentovascularis
Atypical siting or nodular change prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Typical lumbosacral lesions are benign and usually fade by mid-childhood without treatment; aberrant, extensive or syndrome-associated lesions may persist and occasionally point to underlying systemic disease.
pitfalls: Mistaking the blue-grey patch for a bruise and misattributing it to non-accidental injury
Investigating or treating typical, self-limiting lesions unnecessarily
Missing an underlying metabolic disorder in extensive, persistent melanocytosis
Overlooking overlap with naevus of Ito or Ota when lesions occur at unusual sites
